summary: Construct formal power series coefficientwise, recognize their units, and use the first nonzero coefficient to classify every ideal over a field.
keyPoints: Formal multiplication uses finite coefficient sums and agrees with the inverse limit of polynomial truncations.
A series over a field is a unit exactly when its constant coefficient is nonzero.
The order is additive on nonzero products; every nonzero ideal is generated by a power of the formal variable.

summary: Testing finite generation only on prime ideals suffices to prove that a commutative ring is Noetherian.
keyPoints: A maximal non-finitely-generated ideal exists by a chain-union argument.
The ideals I+(a) and (I:a) force that maximal counterexample to be prime.

summary: The intersection of maximal ideals controls invertibility and supplies the unit test used in the general form of Nakayama's lemma.
keyPoints: Every proper ideal of a nonzero commutative ring lies in a maximal ideal.
Elements of one plus the Jacobson radical are units.
For a local ring the Jacobson radical is its unique maximal ideal.

titleEn: Localized Ideals and Adjoining an Inverse
summary: Compute extension, contraction, and saturation for arbitrary ideals, and express inversion of one element by a polynomial quotient.
keyPoints: Every ideal of a localization is extended from its contraction.
Contracting an extended ideal gives its saturation, rather than always the original ideal.
Adjoining an inverse of f gives the same universal property as localization at its powers.

summary: Localization preserves principal ideals and unique factorization by extending ideals and discarding prime factors that become units.
keyPoints: A localization of a PID is a PID.
A prime element becomes either a unit or a prime element after localization.
A localization of a UFD is a UFD, provided zero is not inverted.

titleEn: Coset Actions and the Core of a Subgroup
summary: The kernel of the coset action is an intersection of conjugates and the largest normal subgroup contained in the stabilizer.
keyPoints: The core is the intersection of all conjugates of a subgroup.
Finite index gives a factorial divisibility bound on the core's index.
Index equal to the smallest prime divisor of the group order forces normality.

titleEn: Centers, Centralizers, and the Class Equation
summary: Identify the stabilizers of conjugation, count conjugacy classes, and recognize when a cyclic central quotient forces commutativity.
keyPoints: The centralizer is the stabilizer in the conjugation action.
The finite class equation separates central singleton orbits from noncentral classes.
A group with cyclic quotient by its center is abelian.

titleEn: Centers of p-Groups and Cauchy's Theorem
summary: Apply the class equation to nontrivial finite p-groups and derive Cauchy's theorem from Sylow existence.
keyPoints: The center of a nontrivial finite p-group has order divisible by p.
Sylow existence produces an element of order p whenever p divides the finite group order.

summary: Track the derived series under a quotient map to prove that extensions of solvable groups remain solvable.
keyPoints: Surjections carry each derived-series term onto the corresponding term of the quotient.
Once the derived series enters a solvable normal subgroup, it terminates after finitely many further steps.

summary: Reconcile the commutator-quotient definition of abelianization with its description using all abelian quotient groups.
keyPoints: Every normal subgroup giving an abelian quotient contains the commutator subgroup.
The commutator subgroup itself belongs to that family, so it equals their intersection.

titleEn: Cancellation for Finitely Generated Abelian Groups
summary: Recover prime-power cyclic factors from torsion counts and cancel a common finite-product factor.
keyPoints: The sizes of subgroups annihilated by prime powers recover elementary-divisor multiplicities.
Free rank and those finite torsion counts cancel under a common finitely generated abelian factor.
Finite generation is essential.

summary: Factor one-dimensional characters through abelianization and distinguish finite self-duality from canonical double duality.
keyPoints: Characters into the complex multiplicative group factor through abelianization.
A finite abelian group is isomorphic to its character group, with choices.
Evaluation into the double character group is canonical.

summary: The universal properties of free products, abelianization, and direct sums produce a natural comparison isomorphism.
keyPoints: Abelianization turns a free product of groups into the direct sum of the abelianizations.
The two comparison maps are inverse by uniqueness in the universal properties.

titleEn: A Bound on Intermediate Fields of a Number Field
summary: Apply the existing simple-extension bound after the primitive element theorem, without estimating a normal closure.
keyPoints: A degree-n number field is simple and has at most 2 to the n subfields.

summary: Independent square classes yield a monomial basis, independent sign changes, and many intermediate fields.
keyPoints: Independent square classes give degree 2 to the number of generators.
The Galois group is an elementary abelian 2-group.
Quadratic intermediate fields correspond to nonzero linear forms on that group.

summary: Extend the elementwise notion of separability to algebraic extensions of arbitrary degree and relate it to finite subextensions.
keyPoints: An algebraic extension is separable when every element has a separable minimal polynomial.
The general definition agrees with finite embedding counts.
Characteristic zero gives separability element by element, including infinite extensions.

summary: Use p-powers and the unique-conjugate criterion without dividing infinite field degrees.
keyPoints: Pure inseparability is an elementwise p-power condition in positive characteristic.
An algebraic element is purely inseparable exactly when it has only one distinct conjugate.
Equivalently, the algebraic extension has a unique embedding into an algebraic closure.

titleEn: Fixed Fields of Algebraic Normal Extensions
summary: Finite automorphism orbits give separability over the fixed field, while normality forces that fixed field to be purely inseparable over the original base.
keyPoints: Each algebraic element has a finite orbit even when the automorphism group is infinite.
The distinct-orbit polynomial has fixed coefficients and no repeated roots.
Normality and extension of embeddings force each fixed element to have a unique conjugate over the base.
